ce:list-item.ce:para: Sandblasting pretreatment can effectively remove the adhesive covering the surface of OSB to improve bonding.
The dry bonding shear strength of OSB and Chinese fir was increased by 53 %, 39 %, and 37 % for PRF, PUR, and EPI, respectively.
Delamination rates were reduced to about a half with the original.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The investigation was conducted into the adhesive performance within hybrid cross-laminated timber (HCLT) composed of sandblasted Chinese fir and oriented strand board (OSB) which was originally covered by cured adhesive during the manufacture leading to very fragile bonding. HCLT specimens with three layers were bonded utilizing three structural adhesives which were polyresorcinol formaldehyde (PRF), polyurethane (PUR), and polyisocyanate (EPI). Surface roughness and wettability testing ascertained that sandblasting could effectively change the original resin layer and microtopography on the surface of OSB laminates, significantly modified the level of roughness on the surface, thereby providing a basis for vertical spreading and permeating of the adhesives. Sandblasting pretreatment consistently augmented the dry bonding shear strength about all the three adhesives, achieving the most substantial increases of 53 %, 39 %, and 37 % for PRF, PUR, and EPI, respectively. The pretreatment further reducing delamination rates to about a half in cyclic delamination tests of all three adhesives. Fluorescence microscopy detection of the bonding interfaces revealed a significant increase in adhesive penetration depth which had been further confirmed by the bonding interface thickness measurement. Surface roughness generally had a negative effect on dry shear bonding strength, especially with EPI adhesive, while surface wettability was positively correlated with bonding strength and adhesive layer thickness. This study introduced an environmental and efficient method to enhance the bonding performance of HCLT.

ce:section.ce:para: Cross-laminated timber (CLT) represents a cutting-edge engineering wood product, distinguished by its energy efficiency, environmental sustainability, and a remarkable blend of qualities including high strength, fire resistance, and exceptional shock-absorption capabilities [1]. Consequently, CLT has gained widespread adoption in construction, particularly in mid- to high-rise structures, long-span timber buildings, and mixed-use developments. Typically, CLT comprises a minimum of three layers of solid sawn timber or structural composite lumber with a predominant use of solid wood sawn materials in its manufacturing. However, structural composite boards offer distinct advantages over solid wood sawn timber. For instance, the placement of structural composite panels in the middle layers of CLT serves to mitigate the potential for rolling shear effects within the material. Furthermore, the inclusion of structural composite boards, through careful lamination and bonding, effectively addresses wood defects, leading to uniform and stable mechanical properties. This approach also minimizes the impact of wood anisotropy and inherent defects on the structural integrity of the final product, thus substantially enhancing overall performance [2–4].

In recent years, human activities are grappling with the challenge of wood resource scarcity. In response to the evolving landscape of modern wood construction, there has been a global surge in the utilization of engineered wood products, emphasizing the substitution of solid wood sawn lumber with small-diameter timber for the production of CLT. The development of hybrid cross-laminated timber (HCLT) using domestically abundant structural composite boards, such as oriented strand board (OSB), laminated veneer lumber (LVL), parallel strand lumber (PSL), and laminated strand lumber (LSL), presents significant potential. This approach not only diversifies the available raw materials for CLT production but also promotes local manufacturing practices. Furthermore, OSB, produced from oriented wood strands bonded through hot pressing, often utilizes small-diameter timber or rapidly renewable wood sources, thereby reducing its environmental impact. The relatively straightforward manufacturing process, combined with the diverse availability of raw materials, positions OSB as a cost-effective alternative to solid wood, plywood, LVL, and PSL in the global market [5].

The quality of glued wood composites products is intricately tied to their adhesive properties. With the expanding application of CLT in the construction industry, the effective and safe utilization of structural adhesives becomes foundational to mechanical integrity and performance of CLT. Among the cold curing structural adhesives used on these wood structures, one-component polyurethane (PUR), two-component polyisocyanate emulsion-type adhesive (EPI), and polyresorcinol formaldehyde adhesive (PRF) are the most commonly used adhesives owing to their great bonding performance and easy process properties. The bonding molecular mechanism of one-component PUR adhesive involves the reaction of isocyanate groups with moisture to form amines, which then react with more isocyanates to create strong urea linkages, forming a cross-linked polymer network. This adhesive penetrates the porous wood structure, creating mechanical interlocking while forming urethane bonds with hydroxyl groups in the wood, resulting in a durable, moisture-resistant bond. PRF adhesive bonds wood by reacting resorcinol with formaldehyde to create a network of cross-linked polymers via condensation, which eliminates water during the solidification. This adhesive can establish a strong bond through both mechanical interlocking and hydrogen bonding with the natural hydroxyl groups in wood, ensuring excellent durability and water resistance. The two-component EPI also bonds wood through a combination of mechanical interlocking and chemical cross-linking. The polyvinyl acetate emulsion provides initial adhesion, while the polyisocyanate cross-linker reacts with hydroxyl groups in the wood and emulsion to form strong urethane bonds, creating a durable, moisture-resistant bond. In this study, the above three structural adhesives in commercial use were studied.

Research into the adhesive performance of CLT is gaining increasing importance while ensuring the excellence of its mechanical characteristics. Factors such as the type of adhesive, variation of wood, holding pressure, and curing time, play a crucial role in the adhesive performance [6]. Musah et al. [7] delved into delamination tests of cross-laminated wood blocks subjected to wet-dry cyclic conditions. Their study involved a combination of seven hardwood and two softwood species, constructing two-layers cross-laminated panels using phenol-resorcinol adhesive and melamine-based adhesive. Their findings highlighted the superior gluing durability of mixed hardwood and softwood cross-laminates in wet-dry cycling, the general superiority of phenol-resorcinol adhesive in cyclic delamination tests compared to melamine adhesive, and the direct impact of adhesive viscosity on the adhesive penetration depth into the wood, consequently influencing delamination rates. Purba et al. [8] explored the bonding quality of CLT and glued wood manufactured from oak as well as mixed poplar and oak species, varying bonding pressures and adhesive types. Their research unveiled that CLT or glued laminated wood derived from only oak exhibited higher delamination rates compared to the mixed samples. Nevertheless, sole oak CLT demonstrated superior residual shear strength, with optimal bonding quality achieved with the 0.8 MPa compression pressure and use of the polyurethane resin. Dong et al. [9] studied the bonding performance of bamboo CLT composites, constructed with Spruce-pine-fir (SPF) dimension lumber and bamboo scrimber. Their findings underscored the paramount influence of adhesive type on bonding performance. The optimal manufacturing parameters included the use of phenol resorcinol formaldehyde (PRF) adhesive, an adhesive spreading rate of 250 g/m2, clamping pressure of 1.0 MPa, and clamping time of 420 min. Yusoh et al. [10] investigated the impact of wood species, clamping pressure, and glue spread rate on the strength of CLT joints derived from four tropical hardwood species. Their study revealed that glue spread rate significantly affected CLT bonding shear strength and wood breakage rates, and clamping pressure had no observable effect on CLT gluing performance. However, the performance of the CLT specimens in their study met only the minimum values of the European standard. So there has been a long way to go to study and improve the bonding properties of hybrid CLT.

To enhance the bonding properties of engineering wood products, surface intended modification-based pretreatments of construction laminates was a widely employed strategy. Common methods for improving bonding properties encompass surface sanding [11], surfactant addition [12–14], plasma treatment [15,16], high voltage electrostatic field (HVEF) treatment [17,18], and so on. Sandblasting, a surface treatment technique, involves the high-speed projection of sand or similar granular materials into the surface layer of the processed material. This process effectively removes contaminants, oxidation layers, coatings, and more, resulting in a clean, smooth, and suitably rough surface texture [19]. In the study by Tan et al. [20], a combination of sandblasting and resin pre-coating was employed to enhance the interface bonding strength between carbon fiber-reinforced polymers and aluminum alloy substrates. Results from single lap shear tests revealed that this method led to a remarkable increase in shear strength, surpassing 170.2 %. The performance of the adhesive interface plays a pivotal role in determining the efficacy of engineered wood products, and the manner in which adhesive penetrates the porous wood structure profoundly impacts bonding strength and durability [21,22]. Adhesive penetration has far-reaching implications, influencing the toughness and ultimate strength of bonded components [23,24], as well as compression and shear stiffness [25]. Thus, a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles governing adhesive penetration is indispensable for ensuring effective bonding. Various factors associated with adhesives including resin viscosity, solid content, holding pressure, and curing temperature in conjunction with the structural composition, adhesive consumption, and shape of the interphase collectively determine the extent of stress concentration and the bonding performance [26–28]. Numerous studies have scrutinized adhesive permeability within wood, employing a diverse array of analytical techniques [29]. Methods employed for the investigation of adhesive penetration in wood encompass optical microscopy [30], scanning thermal microscopy [31,32], fluorescence microscopy [33–35], and SEM [36,37]. Among these, fluorescence microscopy and SEM are the most widely utilized. Fluorescence microscopy is used to analyze the penetration of various adhesive types in several kinds of wood-based composites. The advantages of fluorescence microscopy are that it is easy to use, relatively inexpensive, and provides exceptional color contrast [38,39]. In contrast, SEM boasts a spatial resolution approximately hundreds of times higher than that of fluorescence microscopy, offering the benefits of high magnification and an extensive depth of field. Nevertheless, SEM lacks the inherent contrast between phases in grayscale imagery, which can pose challenges in visually distinguishing between wood and adhesive components.

In this study, we employed three structural adhesives including PUR, PEI, and PRF adhesives to fabricate HCLT utilizing Chinese fir and diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI) produced structural OSB. It was found that the dry bonding shear strength of HCLT could not meet the requirements, which was owing to the difficulty of adhesive penetration due to the coverage of the original adhesive resin layer on the OSB surface. To address this challenge, we attempted to remove the original resin coating of the laminate. However, OSB consists of laminated stacks of shavings and common sandpaper sanding cannot uniformly solve shavings with different heights on the surface of OSB, so at last sandblasting pretreatment was used. To assess the effectiveness of this approach, changes in surface characteristics were investigated by performing roughness tests and 3D profile observations on the sandblasted OSB laminates. Concurrently, the contact angle tests were done to analyze the wettability on the laminates. Subsequently, the sandblasted HCLT specimens were tested for bonding and water resistance properties. Further insights were gained through fluorescence microscopy, allowing us to explore the glue interface and adhesive penetration with enhanced clarity and precision.

Structural OSB samples with a density of 0.72 g/cm3 produced with MDI resin and scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) were provided by Hubei Tianxin Wood Structure Co., Ltd. Chinese fir (Cunninghamia lanceolata) samples with a density of 0.42 g/cm3 were bought from Ningyuan Fuyuan wood industry Co., Ltd. White corundum sand was set in various mesh sizes including 60, 120, and 180 and provided by Shanghai Suqin Abrasives Co. Ltd. One-component PUR, two-component EPI, and PRF were selected as the structure adhesives for the HCLT production from Harbin Chengfeng Adhesive Co., Ltd. The information about the three structural adhesives is shown in Table 1.

The OSB and Chinese fir specimens were initially cut into blocks with 300 × 75 × 15 mm. The 300 mm corresponded to the fiber direction of the wood and length direction of the OSB which was mainly the orientation of the large shavings, respectively. The 75 mm correspond to the radial direction of the wood and width of the OSB, while 15 mm corresponded to the OSB thickness and the tangential direction of the wood. The specimens were then stored under controlled conditions at 20 °C and 60 % RH until the moisture content become constant with about 12 %. The sandblasting procedure was conducted within the box-type sandblasting machine (90L8228, TOOLPOWER Tools Co. Ltd) which was linked to the air compressor (OTS-750, Taizhou Otus Industry and Trade Co., Ltd.) operating at a rated exhaust pressure of 0.5 MPa with the 60° processing angle. The sandblasting process involved precise control of the variables. The treatment duration was set with 2, 4, and 6 s based on the rough tests of pre-experiments. The distance parameter between nozzle and OSB surface was set with 6 cm to facilitate the experimental processing, while the 60, 120, and 180 mesh treating particles were also selected according to the pre-tests.

All the wood and OSB samples without any imperfections were chosen for the product of HCLT specimens and testing samples. Structure adhesives were applied evenly to the faces of the prepared laminates using the roller, ensuring optimal coverage. The OSB in the core position of HCLT had been glued on both sides without sizing the first- and third-layers wood. The gummed OSB in the form of a whole board was laid up in the middle and wood was put on both sides with fiber grain perpendicular to the lengthwise of the OSB panel. And then, all the test specimens underwent the cold pressing procedure utilizing the pressing machine (XLB, Qingdao Xincheng Yiming Rubber Machinery Co., Ltd.) and the specific process parameters chosen are detailed in Table 2. The main production process is represented in Fig. 1. The unpretreated OSB and wood produced HCLT was conducted as the control group, while the sandblasting treated OSB with designed parameters were studied detailed here.

The probe roughness measuring instrument TR200 (Mitutoyo, Japan) was used to measure the surface before and after sandblasting treatment in the parallel and perpendicular to lengthwise directions of the OSB samples. Ra (the arithmetical mean deviation of the assessed profile), Rz (maximum height of the profile), RSm (mean width of the profile elements), and RPc (peak count per 1 cm) were chosen to analysis and compared. Two orthogonal directions were tested 5 times, that was, each specimen was tested 10 times, and then the average surface roughness parameters were calculated. The VK-X1000 laser microscope produced by Keyence, Japan was utilized to reveal the 3D profile of the sample surfaces.

For the contact angle measurements, the specimen was placed onto the sample fixture of the contact angle measurement device (Dataphysics, OCA 40, Germany). Deionized water was loaded into a syringe, and the liquid was dispensed uniformly onto the center of the specimen surface using the syringe. Throughout this process, the syringe needle kept perpendicular to the surface and maintained a distance of 2 mm from the surface. The contact angle measuring parameters were configured, and a video recording tool was activated to document the liquid behavior on the surface. The process from the initial contact angle (CAi) to the equilibrium contact angle (CAs) was recorded. Following each measurement, the specimen was repositioned to measure the next point. Five points were randomly even selected from each specimen.

The standard EN 16351-2021[40] served as the reference and the electromechanical universal testing machine (CMT4306, Shenzhen Sansi Testing Machine Co., Ltd.) was used to carry out the adhesive layer shear strength test with 20 specimens in each group. Specimens were placed within a constant temperature and humidity chamber set at 20 °C and 65 % relative humidity to stabilize their quality before conducting the adhesive layer shear strength test. During the tests, a displacement-controlled loading mode was employed, with a loading rate of 5 mm/min. The loading direction remained consistently parallel to the direction of the Chinese fir laminate along the grain, ensuring alignment with standard testing procedures. After the completion of the test, the maximum load in the process of shearing was recorded and noted as Fmax, the calculation is shown in Eq. (1):(1)fv=FmaxAwhere fv is the shear strength of the adhesive layer, MPa; Fmax is the maximum load, N. A is the area of the glued layer, mm2.

According to the standard EN 16351-2021 [40], the decompression and pressurization peeling rate test was conducted on 70 × 70 mm specimens, and 8 specimens were tested in each group. These HCLT specimens underwent a series of treatments, including water impregnation, vacuuming with 70–85 kPa for 5 min, pressurization with 500–600 kPa for 1 h, repeated twice, then drying to restore their initial moisture content. During drying, proper spacing between specimens was maintained, with their wood grain oriented parallel to the airflow. After completion of the test, the delamination length of the adhesive layer of the specimens was determined and the total delamination rate of the adhesive layer was calculated according to Eq. (2):(2)D=lLwhere, D is the total stripping rate, %; l is the total peel length, mm; L is the total length of the adhesive layer, mm. Each group was tested with 20 specimens to calculate the mean and standard deviation value.

For the analysis of adhesive penetration and resin distribution, 5 mm × 5 mm × 30 μm sections were carefully extracted from each HCLT specimen with bonding interface in the middle utilizing an ultramicrotome (LeicaEMUC7, Brunswick, Germany). These sections were then subjected to a staining process using 1 % fluorescent dye Safranine O, where they were immersed for 30 min. Following staining, the sections were sequentially submerged in ethanol solutions of increasing concentrations: 50, 70, 90, and finally 100 %, each for a duration of 10 min to remove excess dye and dehydrate the sections. Subsequently, the stained sections were subjected to observation using a fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX51, Tokyo, Japan).

On the basis of the above obtained fluorescence micrographs of the bonded interface layers, open-source image processing program ImageJ 1.54 g was applied to enhance the images to improve contrast between the adhesive layer and the substrates wood and OSB. The interface should appear as a distinct fluorescent band or layer between two substrates. And then, a line perpendicular to the interface across the bonding layer was draw and the length of the line was converted into the real thickness of the bonding layer using the calibrated scale shown in Fig. 2. Meanwhile, each group with 51 thickness results of the bonding interface at even distributed along sample size 5 mm bonding layer with 100 μm between the adjacent test points was measured and analysis.

The untreated OSB surface exhibited a relative smoothness. Its Ra, Rz, RSm, and RPc were 2.1 μm, 13 μm, 189 μm and 53 (Table 3), respectively. The hot-pressed cured MDI resin concealed the natural structure of wood, showing an original hydrophobic adhesive layer covering the surface with CAi of 114.3°and CAs of 96.2°(Table 4). After designed sandblasting, the grain of the wood strands came out and there was obvious frosted morphology, which indicated that sandblasting could effectively modify the resin layer covering the OSB surface. Particle diameter distributions of the 60, 120, and 180 mesh and relative processed OSB surface 3D profile with the relative different mesh after 4 s were also shown in Fig. 3.

The results of roughness tests in Table 3 showed that sandblasting significantly changed the roughness of the OSB surfaces. Analysis of variance with p <0.05 showed that both particle size and processing time had significant effects on surface roughness parameters. The overall trend showed that the smaller the mesh number of particles, the larger the surface Ra, Rz and RSm after treatment, and of course the the RPc value turned smaller which was inversely proportional to RSm. In the case of the same size particle treatment, the treated surface also became smoother and smoother over time and became basically stable after about 5 s. The large surface roughness caused by 2 s treatment time was mainly due to the influence of non-shedding and prominent particles on the surface. With the extension of treatment time, the original debris were no longer present, replaced by the newly created surface. Therefore, we could control the treatment time with 60, 120, or180 mesh particles to make the Ra of OSB surface within the range of 3.5 to 6.1, 2.3 to 4.6, and 1.2 to 2.8 μm, respectively. The variation of RSm was similar to that of Ra, while the variation of Rz was not particularly obvious, although the overall trend was gradually decreasing, which was mainly due to the large randomness of Rz.

In addition to the surface roughness parameters, the wettability of the surface was particularly important for the bonding properties. Table 4 showed that CAi decreased significantly after the completion of sandblasting process. Among them, the influence of processing time was more significant. Regardless of the mesh number of particles, the 2 s treatment reduced the CAi by almost half and the results located in the range of 55° to 65°. Meanwhile, the 4 s processing time made CAi between 20 and 30°, and the 6 s processing time between 10° and 20°. This was mainly owing to the curing adhesive in the OSB production process was not completely removed when the short treatment time chosen, the longer treatment allowed the underneath fresh wood to be exposed more, and the combination of coarse microstructure made it fallen more. CAs and CAi basically follow the same change trend. After 120 and 180 mesh particle processing 4 s and 60 mesh processing 6 s could reduce CAs to 0°.

The correlation between surface roughness and contact angle is complex and influenced by several factors, including liquid properties, surface energy, and the geometry of the surface structure. Numerous studies have demonstrated that increasing surface roughness could lead to an increase in the contact angle for hydrophobic surfaces which means enhanced hydrophobicity [41–44]. When surfaces treated with specific methods (e.g., coarse sanding, etching) exhibited greater roughness and correspondingly higher contact angles compared to smoother counterparts. Conversely, for hydrophilic surfaces, increased roughness could lead to a decrease in the contact angle, as the liquid can penetrate into the rough surface structure [41,42]. The intrinsic surface energy of the base material also affects the roughness-contact angle relationship. Materials with low surface energy can achieve higher contact angles due to roughness, while high-energy materials may show less sensitivity to roughness changes [42]. In our research, the cured resin in the OSB surface displayed low surface energy, and the exposed pure material surface showed high energy. But the experimental results here showed that the roughness was reduced after treatment especially by prolonging the time, while the contact Angle was also reduced which was in conflict with the above theory. On the one hand, the newly generated OSB surfaces totally showed hydrophilicity, so the roughness had limited effect on the wetting Angle. On the other hand, mainly due to the short treatment time and the penetration of the original OSB adhesive, the treated surface was still mixed with part of the remained MDI resin leading to the surface energy decreasing with treated time.

The results of the dry shear bonding strength tests are displayed in Table 5. Without sandblasting treatment, PRF group had the highest shear strength among the three adhesive groups, measuring 3.86 MPa, which was 13 % and 17 % higher than that of the PUR and EPI, respectively. As we know, PUR and EPI, as pre-polymerized adhesives, were with larger molecular weight and viscosity difficult to flow and penetrate the wood cell wall and only form a low-hardness adhesive layer [45]. However, all the three adhesives exhibited shear strengths lower than the requirement specified in standard EN 16351-2021 [40]. Therefore, new pretreatment methods must be adopted to improve its bonding performance in order to produce eligible HCLT.

After sandblasting, the shear strength of all the specimens basically exceeded the standard value 4.0 MPa except 60 mesh 2 s processed EPI bonding. Among them, the best bonding performance was remained PRF resin, whose highest bonding strength reached 5.92 MPa in the case of 120 mesh treatment 6 s, which got the 53 % increase of the untreated performance. As for PUR and EPI adhesives, their best performance showed 39 % and 37 % higher than untreated samples, reaching 4.76 MPa and 4.53 MPa, respectively. Although the processing conditions for them to achieve the optimal bonding strength were inconsistent, the best samples were all with above 4 s of the processed duration, and the particle size was also biased to more than 120 mesh. The bonding strength of surfaces with larger rough produced by 60 mesh particle treatment with large particles was also adversely affected. Extending the processing time from 4 s to 6 s did not further improve the bonding strength, regardless of the type of adhesive.

Surface topology plays a crucial role in mechanical interlocking and adhesive penetration, which in turn significantly influence bonding strength. The micro and macro-roughness of OSB surfaces after sandblasting treatment could significantly enhance mechanical interlocking between the adhesive and the sub materials. The rough surface provided more surface area for the adhesive to anchor onto, creating a stronger bond. The treated OSB surfaces also displayed its porous structure which allowed for greater adhesive infiltration, which definitely enhanced the overall bonding strength by creating a larger adhesive interface. Although the treatment times of 4 to 6 s here showed very limited difference in all the dry bonding shear strength, there was some difference in surface roughness shown in Table 3. With the extension of treatment time, the surface roughness did decrease but the bonding strength did not decrease, which was mainly owing to the comprehensive embodiment of surface energy and surface morphology. Although the extension of the treatment time leaded to the reduction of roughness, which would lead to the reduction of the bonding interface area, the treatment would also improve the penetration of the resin, and improved the surface energy, which definitely enhance the combination between the new interface and the solidified adhesive.

The results of the positive and negative pressure cyclic delamination tests are presented in Table 6. The delamination rates for PUR, EPI, and PRF without sandblasting treatment were 14.19 %, 15.11 %, and 6.84 %, respectively. The best performance of the PRF group was attributed to the properties of PRF as an in-situ polymerization adhesive. Its ability to diffuse into cell walls prior to curing contributed to the stabilization of the wood interface, thereby mitigating stress concentration within the interface under fluctuating moisture conditions [43]. The sandblasting pretreatment of bonded surface of OSB indicated a general decrease in the delamination rates for all the three structure adhesive. The PUR resin recorded its lowest delamination rate of 7.44 % with a 48 % reduction compared to the unprocessed, when subjected to 180 mesh sand for 4 s. In the case of the EPI adhesion, the minimal delamination rate of 6.99 % with a 53.74 % decrease was observed under the treatment with 60 mesh for 6 s. Noteworthy in the PRF group, 5 sets of test results achieved delamination rates below 5 % which were in compliance with the standard EN 16351-2021[40]. The lowest delamination rate documented was 4.03 %, achieved under the condition of 120 mesh sand for a duration of 4 s.

This reduction could be attributed to two factors. Firstly, the cured adhesive was considerably harder than the wood, and the strain distribution caused by moisture changes occurred within the wood. The sandblasting induced damaged cells on the wood surface acted as a buffer helping to dissipate pressure at the wood-adhesive interface [26]. Secondly, sandblasting removed the original adhesive layer on the OSB surface, enhancing the bonding between the adhesive and wood thereby improving the adhesive durability in HCLT. It is noteworthy that during the delamination testing, delamination occurred as evidenced in two distinct forms: adhesive layer delamination and intra-layer delamination within the OSB. According to the EN16351-2021[40] standard, effective delamination was defined as the ratio of the length of adhesive layer cracking between vertically adjacent laminates to the total length of the adhesive layer. Therefore, the calculation of the delamination rate does not take into account the cracks formed within the layers of the OSB laminate. However, such internal cracks could also affect the application and other physical and mechanical properties of the HCLT materials. Therefore, the influencing factors and variability of the cyclic delamination test results were indeed relatively large.

The fluorescence microscopy of the HCLT gluing interface with and without sandblasting of OSB laminates bonded by the three structural adhesives using the 120 mesh particle for 4 s were shown in Fig. 4. The PRF specimens were not stained owning to the obvious color contrast between the PRF resin and the wood. As shown in Fig. 4a1–c1, the PUR and EPI adhesives were able to penetrate into the surface of the nature Chinese fir wood to a depth with about 1–2 wood cells, while PRF could invaded into 4–5 layers of Chinese fir wood under the action of low viscosity and holding pressure. There were very few penetrative adhesives observed below the OSB surface in the PUR and EPI groups, and the PRF resin also assume shallower penetration observed in the OSB part compare to the nature wood part. When it came to the sandblasting treated bonding interface shown in Fig. 4a2–c2, adhesive penetration could be observed in the OSB part of the PUR and EPI groups and the depth was about 2–3 wood cells. Sandblasting treatment could effectively improve the penetration of adhesive on the laminated surface. After the sandblasting treatment removed the original adhesive resin coating on the OSB surface, the adhesive could directly contact the OSB surface, distributed smoothly on the laminate surface, and penetrated into the cell interior to form the resin nail, therefore improving the shear strength and the water resistance of the adhesion as shown in Fig. 5.

By further measuring the thickness of the bonding interface shown in Table 7, we could find that there were great differences in the formation of the adhesion layers among the three structural adhesives. Among them, the most obvious difference was PRF adhesive which had an easily distinguishable and thickest bonded interface layer. Even though the OSB surface had cured MDI resin to prevent its penetration, the untreated interface thickness had reached 114 μm, which was 50 % higher than the PUR and 24 % than the EPI, owing to its low viscosity. After surface pretreatment, the thickness of the PRF interfaces layer were all greater than 150 μm, and even reached 198 μm after 60 mesh particles are treated for 6 s. In general, the thickness of the bonded interfacial layer before and after treatment was negatively correlated with the viscosity of the three adhesives. There was only 76 μm bonding interface formation in untreated specimens with PUR adhesives at high viscosity, and the maximum thickness after treatment was only 103 μm. The EPI adhesive interface layers thickness was between 100 to 130 μm after surface treatment with medium viscosity. Under the same particle treatment conditions, the thickness of the interface layer tended to increase with the extension of time. There was indeed the remained residual cured resin with 2 s modification that prevented the subsequent penetration of the structural adhesives. With the decrease of particle size, the formation of a new surface with a lower roughness also leaded to the decrease in the thickness of the adhesive interface layer.

Correlation analysis of all the main experimental data was performed to understand the relationships between different variables including surface roughness and wettability parameters, bonding performance parameters, and bonding interface thickness shown in Fig. 6. There was a strong correlation between the four surface roughness parameters with Ra, Rz, and RSm were positively correlated, while RPc was negatively correlated and their correlation coefficients also reached about 0.9 with high significance. Therefore, if we only use Ra to reflect the roughness of the material surface, it is reasonable to a certain extent. The surface wettability here was basically positively correlated with the surface roughness parameters without RPc which was inversely proportional to roughness. This was mainly because the coarser the OSB surface, the more cured adhesive residue it contains, which made its contact angle larger. Roughness had a negative effect on dry shear bonding strength with the three structural adhesives. In particular, EPI adhesive had a higher significant. This was also because the greater the roughness of the surface, the more hot-pressed cured MDI adhesive involved, which of course had a negative impact on the bonding strength. This was consistent with the trend and principle of influence on the thickness of the bonded interface layers. However, for cyclic delamination test, PUR and PRF showed the positive correlation and EPI confirmed a negative relationship. These was mainly due to the high variability of the cyclic delamination testing, and the influence of OSB sample was also obvious, which was worth further exploration to improve to meet the relevant standards. We also confirmed some common conclusion such as the better the surface wettability, the higher the bonding strength of the adhesives and the greater the thickness of the adhesive layer caused by the improvement of permeability.

The commercial structural adhesives PUR, PRF, and EPI were applied to produce HCLT with Chinese fir wood and structural MDI produced OSB. The investigation focused on the influence of sandblasting pretreatment on the OSB surfaces and HCLT bonding performance. To assess the modification within OSB surfaces before and after sandblasting, we conducted roughness measurements, contact angle tests and 3D profile examinations to investigate the effect of the roughness and wetting parameters on the final HCLT bonding properties. Additionally, we carried out vacuum-pressure cyclic delamination tests and dry-state shear tests to evaluate how sandblasting treatment influenced the bonding performance of HCLT specimens. Meanwhile, fluorescence microscopy was employed to analyze adhesive penetration in the samples and the thickness of the bonded interfaces were compared. Our findings revealed that the principle of sandblasting treatment to improve the bonding performance of HCLT was that sandblasting treatment changed the original adhesive layer from the surface of OSB laminates, exposing most of the natural surface of the wood and enhancing the adhesive penetration. Sandblasting effectively reduced the delamination rate of the three adhesives by about half and the PRF group was able to meet the requirements of the EN16351-2021[40] standard after sandblasting. But other two adhesions needed further improvement in the cyclic delamination test. Sandblasting of OSB laminates significantly improved the shear strength of HCLT, with all the groups meeting the 4.0 MPa requirement determined by the EN 16351-2021 standard [40]. In addition, fluorescence microscopy of the glued interface confirmed the influence of the sandblasting treatment on the penetration capacity of the adhesive in the wood which depended on the resin mobility. This study highlighted the potential of sandblasting as an effective, environmentally friendly method for enhancing HCLT bonding durability through wood surface modification.
